newsitem.title: USA: Atwood to head U.S. observers at Nicaragua poll.
newsitem.headline: Atwood to head U.S. observers at Nicaragua poll.

text.p: The United States said Friday it was sending a delegation led by its top aid official to observe presidential elections Oct. 20 in Nicaragua, a key Cold War battleground during the 1980s.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns pledged that the United States would respect the results of the elections, even though one of the candidates is Daniel Ortega, who led the country when relations with Washington were at rock bottom.
Burns said the American delegation would be headed by Brian Atwood, administrator of the U.S. Agency for International Development (AID).

Washington has provided $9 million to help the impoverished Central American country stage the elections, which pit Arnoldo Aleman of the right-wing Liberal Alliance against Ortega, leader of the leftist Sandinista Front.

Burns insisted that Washington was neutral in the vote despite his outspoken criticisms earlier this week of Ortega, who was Nicaraguan leader from 1979-90, a time of civil war between government forces and U.S-backed Contra rebels.

"We are neutral, we're not going to involve ourselves in the political campaign in Nicaragua. That's for the Nicaraguan people to decide on October 20. It's a very important election," Burns told a news briefing.
Asked how he could square that with previous assertions that he could not describe Ortega as a "good democrat", Burns said he was merely being "direct and honest."

"I don't believe if you took a survey of the American people that 99.8 percent of our population would describe him as a good democrat, not with friends like (Libyan leader) Muammar Gaddafi and (Iraqi President) Saddam Hussein, whom he has recently seen," Burns said.

Burns recalled that he and other U.S. officials had also made critical comments about Russian Communist Party candidate Gennady Zyuganov when he stood against Boris Yeltsin in presidential elections last June.
"Had Mr Zyuganov won the election in Russia, I'm sure we would have worked with Mr Zyuganov. We'll respect the outcome of a democratic election in Nicaragua," he said.
"Redemption can occur in some cases. And let's see if it ever does in this one," he added, referring to Ortega.
The United States has cold-shouldered attempts by the Sandinistas to show that they have set aside their Marxist past and want good relations with Washington.

Earlier this week, the State Department demanded that the Sandinistas withdraw a television commercial showing Ortega alongside U.S. Democratic congressman Bill Richardson, saying it was misleading. The Sandinistas rapidly complied.
